lessons.title: Vodka: Neutral Doesn’t Mean Boring

questions.prompt: What legally defines vodka?
questions.insight: Vodka is defined by neutrality (minimal dominant aroma/flavor) and is typically bottled around 40% ABV. Juniper = gin; barrel-aged grain = whiskey; fruit liqueur = sweetened modifier.

questions.prompt: What is the most common base ingredient for vodka?
questions.insight: Wheat is common and often yields a soft mouthfeel. Agave points to tequila; molasses to rum; grapes to brandy.

questions.prompt: Select possible vodka base ingredients:
questions.insight: Vodka can be made from many fermentables (grain, potato, corn). Juniper is a botanical used to define gin, not a vodka base.

questions.prompt: Why is vodka considered “neutral”?
questions.correct_text: Because it is distilled and filtered to remove strong flavors and aromas.
questions.insight: Neutral means minimal dominant flavor—differences show up more in texture, mouthfeel, and finish than big aromas.

questions.prompt: Match the base to its typical texture:
questions.insight: Vodka differences are often felt more than tasted—base choice influences body and perceived smoothness.

questions.prompt: A guest says, “Vodka all tastes the same.” What’s the best response?
options: “Actually, base ingredients affect texture and smoothness.”
questions.insight: You keep rapport and educate without arguing. It reframes vodka as texture-driven rather than flavorless.

questions.prompt: Why is vodka ideal for infusions?
options: It’s neutral and highlights added flavors
questions.insight: Neutral base = the infused ingredient becomes the headline, not the spirit.

questions.prompt: Put vodka production steps in order:
questions.insight: Filtration/refining typically follows distillation; bottling comes last.

questions.prompt: What most impacts vodka smoothness?
questions.insight: Production quality drives smoothness—packaging doesn’t change the liquid.

questions.prompt: Name one cocktail where vodka structure matters.
questions.insight: In spirit-forward or lightly flavored builds, vodka’s texture and finish become more noticeable.

lessons.title: Gin & Botanicals Breakdown

questions.prompt: What botanical must legally be present in gin?
questions.insight: Juniper defines gin. Without juniper, it isn’t gin—other botanicals are optional additions.

questions.prompt: What does “London Dry” indicate?
questions.insight: London Dry is a production style, not a location. It restricts sweetening/flavor additions after distillation.

questions.prompt: Select common gin botanicals:
questions.insight: Molasses is used to make rum; botanicals are aromatic plants used to flavor gin.

questions.prompt: Match gin styles to profile:
questions.insight: Navy Strength refers to ABV (~57%), not sweetness—style impacts how you build and dilute.

questions.prompt: Why does gin pair well with citrus?
questions.correct_text: Because citrus enhances and highlights botanical brightness.
questions.insight: Citrus oils amplify gin’s botanical lift and keep the drink tasting bright.

questions.prompt: A guest says gin tastes “too piney.” What do you recommend?
options: Switch to a citrus-forward or floral gin
Tell them gin isn’t for them
questions.insight: Not all gins are heavy juniper—modern gins lean citrus/floral, keeping the guest in the category.

questions.prompt: What mixer defines the most classic gin serve?
questions.insight: Tonic’s quinine bitterness complements botanicals; soda is neutral and won’t ‘complete’ the same way.

questions.prompt: Put gin production in order:
questions.insight: Gin starts as neutral spirit—botanicals become the identity during redistillation.

questions.prompt: Typical ABV of Navy Strength gin?
questions.insight: Historically tied to gunpowder ignition tests—expect more intensity and adjust dilution accordingly.

questions.prompt: Name one herb that enhances gin cocktails.
questions.insight: Fresh herbs mirror gin’s botanical complexity and add aromatic top notes.

lessons.title: Rum Styles

questions.prompt: Rum is produced from what base ingredient?
questions.insight: Rum comes from sugarcane. Agricole rum uses fresh cane juice; most rum uses molasses.

questions.prompt: Dark rum gets its color primarily from:
questions.insight: Traditional color comes from barrel aging. Some producers add coloring, but aging is the core driver.

questions.prompt: Select rum styles:
questions.insight: These are common style buckets—overproof refers to strength (usually 50%+ ABV).

questions.prompt: Match region to common style:
questions.insight: Fermentation and blending traditions differ by region and strongly shape flavor.

questions.prompt: What does “funk” mean in rum?
questions.insight: Think overripe tropical fruit notes—powerful aroma that stands up in cocktails.

questions.prompt: Guest wants tropical but not too sweet. What build works?
questions.insight: A rum highball stays refreshing and avoids sugar overload while keeping flavor.

questions.prompt: Agricole rum is made from:
questions.insight: Agricole is grassy/vegetal compared with molasses-based rum’s deeper sweetness.

questions.prompt: Rum aging sequence:
questions.insight: Blending is common to maintain consistency and balance across barrels.

questions.prompt: Overproof rum usually exceeds:
questions.insight: Overproof needs dilution awareness—small changes in ice/time matter more.

questions.prompt: Name a classic rum cocktail ratio.
questions.insight: The Daiquiri is the template: spirit + sweet + acid in balance.

lessons.title: Tequila & Agave Spectrum

questions.prompt: Tequila must be made from which plant?
questions.insight: Tequila is specifically Blue Weber agave; other agave spirits can use different varieties.

questions.prompt: Tequila is protected by region in:
questions.insight: Protected designation of origin—like Champagne—anchors authenticity.

questions.prompt: Select tequila categories:
questions.insight: Tequila categories describe aging; London Dry is gin terminology.

questions.prompt: Match type to aging:
questions.insight: Aging adds vanilla/spice and tends to smooth alcohol perception.

questions.prompt: What flavor does agave naturally contribute?
questions.insight: Agave sweetness is distinct—more earthy than sugarcane.

questions.prompt: Guest says tequila tastes harsh. Best move?
questions.insight: Reposado’s barrel time softens edges and adds warmth, often winning skeptical guests.

questions.prompt: Mezcal differs from tequila primarily because:
options: It can use different agave and is often smoked
questions.insight: Smoke often comes from underground roasting; agave variety and region can differ widely.

questions.prompt: Tequila production:
questions.insight: Cooking converts starches to fermentable sugars—crucial for flavor and yield.

questions.prompt: “100% agave” on the label means:
questions.insight: Mixto tequila can include other sugars; 100% agave signals purity of fermentable source.

questions.prompt: Classic tequila cocktail ratio?
questions.insight: Margarita = sour template—tequila + sweet + acid.

lessons.title: Whiskey Families

questions.prompt: Bourbon must contain at least how much corn?
questions.insight: 51% corn minimum drives bourbon’s sweetness. Rye-heavy profiles indicate different styles.

questions.prompt: Rye whiskey is typically known for which flavor profile?
questions.insight: Rye’s spice is its calling card. Peat smoke is more associated with some Scotch.

questions.prompt: Select recognized whiskey families:
questions.insight: Tequila is agave-based, not a whiskey family.

questions.prompt: Match style to common trait:
questions.insight: These are useful ‘default expectations’ to guide recommendations and pairings.

questions.prompt: What gives Scotch its smoky character?
questions.insight: The smoke comes from malting/drying, not barrel aging.

questions.prompt: A guest wants bold and dry, not sweet. What do you recommend?
questions.insight: Rye’s spice feels drier and more assertive than bourbon’s sweet oak profile.

questions.prompt: Whiskey gets its color primarily from:
questions.insight: Distillate is clear before the barrel—wood contact creates color and flavor.

questions.prompt: Put whiskey maturation in order:
questions.insight: Aging integrates and softens spirit character; bottling comes last.

questions.prompt: What is the “angel’s share”?
questions.insight: A portion evaporates through the barrel during aging—this is the angel’s share.

questions.prompt: Name a classic spirit-forward whiskey cocktail.
questions.insight: Spirit-forward builds highlight barrel influence, texture, and finish.

lessons.notes: Enhanced feedback format: each question includes a corrective insight.

lessons.title: Brandy & Fortified Wines

questions.prompt: Brandy is distilled from:
questions.insight: Brandy is distilled wine—fruit origin shapes softness and aroma.

questions.prompt: Cognac must come from:
questions.insight: Cognac is geographically protected; not all brandy is Cognac.

questions.prompt: Select fortified wines:
questions.insight: Fortified wines are wine strengthened with spirit—used as modifiers.

questions.prompt: Fortified wine to common use:
questions.insight: Fortified wines bring flavor complexity without base-spirit strength.

questions.prompt: Why should vermouth be refrigerated after opening?
questions.insight: Old vermouth is a top cause of flat, dull martinis.

questions.prompt: A Martini tastes flat. What’s a likely cause?
questions.insight: Oxidized vermouth loses brightness and herbal lift, making the drink taste tired.

questions.prompt: Fortified wine differs from regular wine because:
questions.insight: Fortification increases ABV and changes stability/structure.

questions.prompt: Fortification process:
questions.insight: Spirit is added after fermentation to fortify; flavoring/aging comes before bottling.

questions.prompt: Typical vermouth ABV is around:
questions.insight: Higher than wine, lower than spirits—perfect as a structural modifier.

questions.prompt: Why are fortified wines considered modifiers?
questions.correct_text: They adjust flavor and balance rather than act as the main alcohol.
questions.insight: They shape the profile (sweetness, bitterness, herbs) without dominating the drink.

lessons.title: Liqueurs & Modifiers Explained

questions.prompt: What defines a liqueur?
questions.insight: Liqueurs are sweetened spirits—sugar is the defining feature.

questions.prompt: Typical liqueur ABV range?
questions.insight: Most liqueurs sit below base spirits; they modify and sweeten.

questions.prompt: Select liqueur categories:
questions.insight: Categories help you predict how the modifier will behave in balance.

questions.prompt: Match liqueur to cocktail:
questions.insight: Classic specs rely on specific modifiers—swap carefully or you break the structure.

questions.prompt: Why can too much liqueur unbalance a drink?
questions.correct_text: It can over-sweeten and overpower structure.
questions.insight: Too much sugar dulls acidity and makes the drink feel heavy and flat.

questions.prompt: Drink tastes flat and one-dimensional. What helps?
questions.insight: Bitterness adds contrast and depth—often the missing layer.

questions.prompt: Amaro is typically:
questions.insight: Amaro sits in the bitter-herbal family, adding complexity and length to finishes.

questions.prompt: Modifier logic sequence:
questions.insight: Build structure first; final balance is where you fine-tune.

questions.prompt: Cream liqueurs should be stored:
questions.insight: Cream-based products spoil faster—cold storage protects quality.

questions.prompt: Name one function of orange liqueur.
questions.correct_text: Adds citrus sweetness and bridges flavors.
questions.insight: It connects spirit, acid, and sweetness—especially in sour templates like Margaritas.

lessons.title: Understanding Oak & Aging

questions.prompt: Oak aging often adds which flavor?
questions.insight: Vanillin and toasted wood compounds create the classic vanilla/spice profile.

questions.prompt: Charred barrels create:
questions.insight: Charring caramelizes wood sugars, contributing caramel/toffee notes.

questions.prompt: Aging affects:
questions.insight: ABV often drops slightly; aging mainly changes color, aroma, and mouthfeel.

questions.prompt: Aging duration to impact:
questions.insight: Longer aging increases integration and depth—but can also add dryness.

questions.prompt: Why do smaller barrels age faster?
questions.correct_text: More wood surface contact per volume.
questions.insight: More contact speeds extraction and oxidation effects.

questions.prompt: Guest wants a smoother option. What helps?
questions.insight: Aging and oxidation typically soften harsh edges and add roundness.

questions.prompt: New oak barrels are required for:
questions.insight: Bourbon regulations require new charred oak, creating its signature profile.

questions.prompt: Barrel influence flow:
questions.insight: Extraction + oxidation over time creates integrated flavor.

questions.prompt: Oxidation during aging generally:
questions.insight: Slow oxygen exposure mellows alcohol heat and rounds flavors.

questions.prompt: Why do aged spirits pair well with spice?
questions.correct_text: They share warm flavor compounds like vanilla and clove.
questions.insight: Pairing works when flavor families overlap—oak warmth + baking spice is a classic match.

lessons.title: Pairing Spirits with Ingredients

questions.prompt: Tequila most naturally pairs with which ingredient?
questions.insight: Agave + citrus is a classic structural pairing—lime balances earthy sweetness.

questions.prompt: Bourbon complements which flavor best?
questions.insight: Maple amplifies bourbon’s vanilla/caramel notes; it’s harmony, not conflict.

questions.prompt: Select ingredients that pair naturally with gin:
questions.insight: Gin likes bright/herbal pairings; chocolate is heavy and harder to balance.

questions.prompt: Match spirit to ideal pairing:
questions.insight: Pairings work by complementing core notes or adding structured contrast.

questions.prompt: Why does acid balance sweetness in cocktails?
questions.correct_text: Acid cuts heaviness and prevents the drink from tasting flat.
questions.insight: Acid adds ‘life’—without it, sweet drinks become syrupy and dull.

questions.prompt: A guest wants something refreshing but strong. What’s your move?
questions.insight: Highballs keep perceived strength while tasting lighter due to carbonation and controlled dilution.

questions.prompt: What ingredient adds contrast to sweet rum drinks?
questions.insight: Contrast prevents cloying sweetness—lime sharpens and rebalances.

questions.prompt: Put pairing logic in correct order:
questions.insight: Start with base + pairing logic, then tune sweetness and balance at the end.

questions.prompt: Which pairing is structurally classic (not random)?
questions.insight: Tequila + lime is classic sour structure; it’s a proven balance relationship.

questions.prompt: Name one herb that lifts whiskey cocktails.
questions.insight: Herbs add aromatic lift that contrasts warm oak and spice.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Build by Flavor

questions.prompt: Guest loves smoky food and bold flavors. What spirit do you build with?
questions.insight: Smoke mirrors smoke—use mezcal to match bold flavor expectations.

questions.prompt: If a cocktail tastes too bitter, you should adjust with:
questions.insight: Sweetness softens bitterness. Ice can help via dilution, but sweetness is the primary counterweight.

questions.prompt: A balanced cocktail usually includes:
questions.insight: Most classics rely on a strong/sweet/sour backbone—even when one element is subtle.

questions.prompt: Define “harmony” in cocktail building.
questions.correct_text: Flavors complement each other without one overpowering.
questions.insight: Harmony is controlled balance—everything is present, nothing dominates.

questions.prompt: Match flavor preference to spirit:
questions.insight: This is how you translate guest language into fast, confident recommendations.

questions.prompt: Put build sequence in order:
questions.insight: Dilution is a finishing lever—use it to fine-tune after structure is set.

questions.prompt: What prevents a cocktail from tasting flat?
questions.insight: Acidity gives lift and definition—sweetness alone often tastes dull.

questions.prompt: Judge says your cocktail feels “unbalanced.” First thing you check?
questions.insight: Check structure first. If ratio is wrong, everything else is cosmetic.

questions.prompt: Oak-aged spirits typically pair well with:
questions.insight: Oak brings vanilla/clove/baking spice notes—warm spices reinforce that family.

questions.prompt: Name two signs a pairing succeeded.
questions.insight: Success shows in the finish: integrated flavors, clean aftertaste, no sharp spikes.
